newsitem.title: USA: Top tobacco lawyer attends RJR meeting - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Top tobacco lawyer attends RJR meeting - analysts.

text.p: There was an unusual player at RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.'s meeting with Wall Street analysts Wednesday -- the top lawyer for its R.J. Reynolds Tobacco unit -- but he declined to comment on reports of talks aimed at settling massive lawsuits against the industry.
Charles Blixt, senior vice president and general counsel at R.J. Reynolds, joined RJR Nabisco Chairman Steven Goldstone and other officials at the meeting, people attending said.

Blixt spoke briefly about the legal landscape facing RJR but little information was revealed about the talks, industry analysts who attended the meeting said. Still, they said Blixt's presence in itself was significant.
One analyst said the impression he got from the meeting was that the company "clearly remains amenable to pursuing a reasonable compromise" to the flood of litigation.
But, he added, Blixt was "tight-lipped" about the situation.
"He actually didn't even say they were in negotiations," said another analyst. "He said, 'It's been rumored that we are in talks, but we're not going to comment about it.'"

Tobacco shares soared last week when news broke that talks had started between the Philip Morris Cos. Inc. and RJR, the No. 1 and No. 2 U.S. cigarette makers, and their opponents in the so-called Tobacco Wars.

The first round of talks on a possible settlement of litigation ended last week in Virginia and no date for another round of talks has been scheduled, state officials and lawyers involved in the talks said last week.
Pennsylvania and Missouri Wednesday became the 24th and 25th states to sue the industry.

The tobacco industry has been besieged from all flanks in the last two years with lawsuits seeking billions of dollars filed by individuals and groups as well as state attorneys general suing for reimbursement of state Medicaid funds spent treating tobacco-related illnesses.
Also clouding the industry's horizon is the long-awaited verdict by the federal judge hearing the tobacco industry's challenge to the onset of federal regulation.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration officially began oversight of the industry on Feb. 28, and its regulation, if upheld in court, will change forever the way tobacco companies market, advertise and sell cigarettes.
Judge William Osteen's decision, twice delayed already, is expected on Friday morning.
RJR's meeting was closed to the media.

Blixt's invitation to the meeting, and RJR's nod to its legal troubles, came the day before the annual shareholders meeting of Philip Morris in Richmond, Va. It was not clear whether Philip Morris might broach the subject of the settlement talks at its meeting on Thursday.
